🟡 Blue Ridge Foodshed Fund

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website

Blue Ridge Foodshed Trust emerged in the aftermath of Hurricane Helen as a response to the mounting instability of the global food system and the deep vulnerabilities of rural communities. The Trust's mission is to localize food systems by supporting small-scale farmers, building regenerative distribution infrastructure, and addressing food access through community-centered investment.

Bioregional Context

The Blue Ridge bioregion spans the ancient Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States, encompassing parts of Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee. Characterized by temperate forests, rolling hills, and biodiverse watersheds, the region has long supported resilient agricultural traditions and community-based food systems.

Background


The Blue Ridge Mountains are among the oldest and most biodiverse landscapes on Earth—over 1.2 billion years old, older than the Atlantic Ocean. Cherokee people and their ancestors have stewarded these mountains for roughly 12,000 years. In September 2024, Hurricane Helene tore through the region and exposed a structural tension: western North Carolina still hosts more than 5,000 family farms, numerous aggregators and distributors, and 40 farmers' markets, yet only about 4% of food purchased locally is produced in the region—underscoring how fragile long supply chains are and why many residents are recommitting to bioregional food sovereignty.

Origins and Network


The Blue Ridge Foodshed Trust was formed as a nonprofit corporation with a mission to rapidly localize the regional food supply. The Trust brings funding and resources into the region through trusted relationships with mission-aligned partners. Rooted in the Western North Carolina community, the Trust serves as a valuable intermediary with deep knowledge of the foodshed's challenges, needs, and assets.

Activities

🔸

Farm Food Access Program

The Farm Food Access Program is the Trust’s lead intervention: it pays farmers for food that is then prepared or boxed for community resource centers across six counties—getting dollars onto farms while feeding neighbors through trusted front-line organizations. The design grew from an eight-week pilot backed by a $1 million American Red Cross grant. The theory of change is straightforward—pay producers first, widen the program, and over time reduce dependence on one-off disaster and charity dollars by knitting in schools, institutions, and households as reliable buyers, supported by storytelling that builds demand for local food. Operations lean on Fastroots, a platform for spotting needs, coordinating resources, tracking impact, and sharing transparent, community-held data.

🔸

WNC Food Hub Collaborative

The WNC Food Hub Collaborative is a newly formed group of 10 participating food hubs across the region that collectively purchase from hundreds of local farms. This existing network of aggregation, storage, and distribution capacity provides the foundation upon which a truly integrated regional food system can be built. The Trust works to strengthen and integrate this local food supply chain, reducing inefficiencies, building infrastructure, and expanding capacity.

🔸

Institutional and Commercial Purchasing

Schools, universities, and hospitals could anchor steady demand for regional farms, but procurement rules, food-safety expectations, and thin coordination often block uptake. The Trust is bundling responses: procurement subsidies that reimburse institutional and commercial buyers for verified local purchases; investment in aggregation and food-safety capacity so farms can meet buyers where compliance is non-negotiable; and digital links between hubs and institutions to cut administrative friction.

🔸

Blue Ridge Community Land Agreements

Recognizing that land access is a major barrier for small-scale and BIPOC farmers in the region, the Trust is developing a land strategy based on long-term stewardship rather than speculative ownership. The team is working with landowners in three target landscapes who are willing to enter into long-term agreements that prioritize food production and ecological regeneration. These regenerative land trusts will acquire and permanently protect farmland at risk of development, provide affordable land access to farmers through below-market rates, and ensure long-term affordability for local growers while scaling regional production capacity. The agreements may include community easements, stewardship covenants, or lease-to-own models that favor equity, regenerative production, and generational succession.

🔸

Blue Ridge Foodshed Capital Infrastructure

The Trust is partnering with Abundance Capital to administer the Blue Ridge Foodshed Fund—a catalytic donor-advised fund (DAF). This multi-donor fund receives tax-deductible grants from public, private, and corporate donors, creating a capital pool for grants, zero/low-interest loans, and return-based investments. Returns flow back into the Fund to be reinvested in more initiatives. The team is identifying catalytic projects in three specific landscape clusters across the region. Potential investments include local processing and aggregation centers, mobile market units, cold storage solutions, and co-located services for farmers and food entrepreneurs.

🔸

Producer-Centered Governance Design

A core tenet of the Foodshed Trust model is that producers must play a central role in funding decisions, infrastructure design, and enterprise development. The organization is hosting a series of listening sessions and design workshops with producers across the region to co-create these governance models. Over time, these governance frameworks will be embedded into the operation of the Trust's capital vehicles and community land tools.

Vision and Legacy


Localizing western North Carolina’s food system offers measurable returns in four areas: economic vitality, public health, ecological repair, and community resilience. The Trust treats those returns as mutually reinforcing—farm income, eater access, watershed health, and civic capacity rising together when capital, land, and governance align around producers.
